Question 1

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of increasing x. When the displacement of P from the origin O is xm, its velocity is vm/s and its acceleration is 4xm/s2. If P has a displacement of 2m when its velocity is 8m/s, find v in terms of x.

a
v(x)=85x2+21
b
v(x)=2x2
c
v(x)=x2+4
d
v(x)=2x2+1
e
v(x)=2x2+12
Submit

decision.explanation: Using a=v dv/dx gives v dv=4x dx, so v^2=4x^2+C. At x=2, v=8, hence C=48. Since the particle moves in the direction of increasing x, v is positive, giving v(x)=2√(x^2+12).

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $4x\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $2\,m$ when its velocity is $8\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14064798/assets/017463f3ac8abac9c2b00c4d9a715a4109a5f4bc1b070e0a12c4d3a7bac64351.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4x\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4x.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x=\int 4x\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=2\,\text{m}$ when $v=8\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =2(2)^{2}+C \\ C & =32-8 \\ C & =24\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+24 \\ {v}^{2} & =4{x}^{2}+48 \\ {v}^{2} & =4({x}^{2}+12) \\ v & =\pm 2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+12}.
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4x.

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x=\int 4x\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=2\,\text{m}$ when $v=8\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(8)^{2} & =2(2)^{2}+C \\ C & =32-8 \\ C & =24\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+24 \\ {v}^{2} & =4{x}^{2}+48 \\ {v}^{2} & =4({x}^{2}+12) \\ v & =\pm 2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+12}.
$$

decision.explanation: Acceleration toward the origin gives v dv/dx=-2e^{-x}. Integrating yields v²=4e^{-x}+C; x=0 and v=2 give C=0. Taking the positive velocity, dx/dt=2e^{-x/2}, so d(e^{x/2})/dt=1. The initial position gives e^{x/2}=t+1, hence x(t)=2ln(t+1).

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $2{e}^{-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=2\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14064798/assets/ad437638f22672a10a183f1521929637f8d43725f37a9736c569516232e7c468.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $2{e}^{-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2{e}^{-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-2{e}^{-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -2{e}^{-x}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =2{e}^{0}+K \\ K & =2-2 \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x} \\ {v}^{2} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ v & =\pm 2{e}^{-x/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=2{e}^{-x/2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2{e}^{-x/2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2{e}^{-x/2} \\ {e}^{x/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2 \\ \int {e}^{x/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{x/2}\text{d}x & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ 2{e}^{x/2} & =2t+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{x/2} & =t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
{e}^{x/2}=t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x/2} & =t+1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x/2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1) \\ \frac{x}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1) \\ x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1).\end{aligned}

Therefore,

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing x, we have that v(x)>0, so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

v(x)=2e−x/2.

Now, we know that v=dxdt. Therefore, we have the equation dxdt=2e−x/2.

content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $2{e}^{-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=2\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14064798/assets/ad437638f22672a10a183f1521929637f8d43725f37a9736c569516232e7c468.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $2{e}^{-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2{e}^{-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-2{e}^{-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -2{e}^{-x}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =2{e}^{0}+K \\ K & =2-2 \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x} \\ {v}^{2} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ v & =\pm 2{e}^{-x/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=2{e}^{-x/2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2{e}^{-x/2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2{e}^{-x/2} \\ {e}^{x/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2 \\ \int {e}^{x/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{x/2}\text{d}x & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ 2{e}^{x/2} & =2t+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{x/2} & =t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
{e}^{x/2}=t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x/2} & =t+1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x/2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1) \\ \frac{x}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1) \\ x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since dx/dt=3x, separating variables and integrating gives ln(x)=3t+C, hence x(t)=Ae^{3t}. The initial condition x(0)=2 gives A=2, so x(t)=2e^{3t}.

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14064798/assets/efdb69673b4088d3c021d78282642ff7abc57158e23704cd3d5e7ff2559cbdbb.png)

We're given that the velocity function $v(x)$ is

$$
v(x)=3x.
$$

We know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=3x.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =3x \\ \frac{1}{3x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{3x}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{3x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x| & =t+K \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|x| & =3t+3K \\ x & ={e}^{3t+3K} \\ x & =C{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=2$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=2,$ and the particular solution is

$$
x(t)=2{e}^{3t}.
$$

$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ its acceleration is $2(x+2)^{3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=4\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t$ where $t\in [0,\frac{1}{4}].$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14064798/assets/ba9988a12d1c70c43a6a010c3578850fe79a9bca01309884fe981b3f7cca512c.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $2(x+2)^{3}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2(x+2)^{3}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2(x+2)^{3}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 2(x+2)^{3}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+2)^{4}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=4\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+2)^{4}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(0+2)^{4}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+2)^{4} \\ {v}^{2} & =(x+2)^{4} \\ v & =\pm (x+2)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=(x+2)^{2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=(x+2)^{2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(x+2)^{2} \\ \frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 1\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}}\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ -\frac{1}{x+2} & =t+C \\ \frac{1}{x+2} & =-t-C.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=-\frac{1}{2},$ and the particular solution is

$$
\frac{1}{x+2}=-t+\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+2} & =-t+\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{x+2} & =\frac{1-2t}{2} \\ x+2 & =\frac{2}{1-2t} \\ x & =\frac{2}{1-2t}-2 \\ x & =\frac{4t}{1-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

A particle P moves along the x-axis in the direction of increasing x. When the displacement of P from the origin O is xm, its acceleration is 2(x+2)3m/s2. Initially, P is at the origin O and has velocity v=4m/s. Find x as a function of time t where t∈[0,14].

a
 x(t)=t1−t
b
 x(t)=t21−2t
c
 x(t)=t−4t2
d
 x(t)=2t−t2
e
 x(t)=4t1−2t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P is 2(x+2)3m/s2, we have dvdt=2(x+2)3.

Using the fact that

dvdt=ddx(12v2)

we can rewrite our equation as

ddx(12v2)=2(x+2)3.

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to x, we have ∫ddx(12v2)dx=∫2(x+2)3dx

which gives the general solution

12v2=12(x+2)4+K.

Now, since v=4m/s when x=0m, we can find the value of the constant K, as follows: 12v2=12(x+2)4+K12(4)2=12(0+2)4+K8=8+KK=0

Therefore,

12v2=12(x+2)4v2=(x+2)4v=±(x+2)2.

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing x, we have that v(x)>0, so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

v(x)=(x+2)2.

Now, we know that v=dxdt. Therefore, we have the equation dxdt=(x+2)2.

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to t, we have

dxdt=(x+2)21(x+2)2dxdt=1∫1(x+2)2dxdtdt=∫1dt∫1(x+2)2dx=∫dt−1x+2=t+C1x+2=−t−C.

We're given that x=0 when t=0. Therefore, C=−12, and the particular solution is

1x+2=−t+12.

Finally, writing x in terms of t, we have

1x+2=−t+121x+2=1−2t2x+2=21−2tx=21−2t−2x=4t1−2t.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option e. For x(t)=4t/(1-2t), x(0)=0, x'(t)=4/(1-2t)^2, and x''(t)=16/(1-2t)^3=2(x+2)^3. Thus the initial velocity is 4 and the acceleration is correct throughout [0,1/4]. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option b.

content.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ its acceleration is $2(x+2)^{3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=4\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t$ where $t\in [0,\frac{1}{4}].$
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14064798/assets/ba9988a12d1c70c43a6a010c3578850fe79a9bca01309884fe981b3f7cca512c.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $2(x+2)^{3}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2(x+2)^{3}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2(x+2)^{3}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 2(x+2)^{3}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+2)^{4}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=4\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+2)^{4}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(0+2)^{4}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+2)^{4} \\ {v}^{2} & =(x+2)^{4} \\ v & =\pm (x+2)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=(x+2)^{2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=(x+2)^{2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(x+2)^{2} \\ \frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 1\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{(x+2)^{2}}\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}t \\ -\frac{1}{x+2} & =t+C \\ \frac{1}{x+2} & =-t-C.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=-\frac{1}{2},$ and the particular solution is

$$
\frac{1}{x+2}=-t+\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+2} & =-t+\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{x+2} & =\frac{1-2t}{2} \\ x+2 & =\frac{2}{1-2t} \\ x & =\frac{2}{1-2t}-2 \\ x & =\frac{4t}{1-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since x>0 and acceleration points toward O, a=-3^{1-x}ln(3). Using v dv/dx=a and integrating gives v²/2=3^{1-x}+C. At x=2, v²=8, so C=4-1/3=11/3. At x=1, v²=2(1+11/3)=28/3. Motion is toward decreasing x, so v=-√(28/3)≈-3.1 m/s.

after.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of decreasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is ${3}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3\,{m/s}^{2}$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $v=-2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=1\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14064798/assets/3c5450b18c5dc58b082faadf4086b6a21c0c9b55afb016090147609a2ccfe719.png)

Since the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${3}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-{3}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-{3}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int [-{3}^{1-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3]\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={3}^{1-x}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=-2\sqrt{2}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(-2\sqrt{2})^{2} & ={3}^{1-2}+C \\ 4 & =\frac{1}{3}+C \\ C & =\frac{11}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={3}^{1-x}+\frac{11}{3} \\ {v}^{2} & =2({3}^{1-x}+\frac{11}{3}) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({3}^{1-x}+\frac{11}{3})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)<0,$ so we can discard the positive square root. Therefore,

$$
v=-\sqrt{2({3}^{1-x}+\frac{11}{3})}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =-\sqrt{2({3}^{1-1}+\frac{11}{3})} \\  & =-\sqrt{\frac{28}{3}} \\  & ≈-3.1\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

Since the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle P is 31−xln⁡3m/s2 and is directed toward O, we have dvdt=−31−xln⁡3.

Therefore, 12v2=31−x+113v2=2(31−x+113)v=±2(31−x+113).
